La rondeña, de principios del XIX y de la tierra del Tobalo, es la pieza con que muchos guitarristas abren sus conciertos; la jabera, ruda y difícil, debe su nombre a una vendedora de habas y está casi perdida; los verdiales, de probable raíz morisca, apenas han cambiado y conservan la panda con violín, panderos, chinchines y cañas para la fiesta de san Juan.

scenes.name: Los romances
scenes.desc: El flamenco distingue una docena de palos (romances, tonás, siguiriyas, soleares, tangos, cantiñas, cantes de Levante, fandangos, cantes de Málaga, ida y vuelta, aflamencados e híbridos), cada uno con sus estilos y sus creadores. Los básicos, los más antiguos, empiezan por el romance, la canción española más vieja transmitida oralmente, que los gitanos hicieron suya: es el verdadero punto de origen del cante. También llamados corridos, son las únicas coplas con continuidad narrativa (historias románticas, caballerescas o moriscas) y se cantan a palo seco, sin acompañamiento; con guitarra toman el son de la soleá por bulerías. Washington Irving los oyó en 1829 como «tonadas rudas y sencillas». Hoy casi no se cantan. José Blas Vega grabó en 1971 en el Puerto de Santa María dieciséis romances primitivos de siete intérpretes, todos gitanos, y los dividió en los de flores y Blancaflor, los carolingios, los del Cid, los de Bernardo el Carpio y los moriscos, como el de Zaide; su parentesco con tonás, carceleras, deblas y martinetes es evidente.

scenes.name: Los tanguillos de Cádiz
scenes.desc: Vinculados al carnaval de Cádiz, son el soporte de chirigotas, coros y murgas; cantados en grupo pierden su naturaleza flamenca, que es individual, aunque como baile la conservan. Hay constancia de los «tangos graciosos» del barrio de La Viña en 1779, en la tonadilla La anónima de Tomás Abril, y el tango americano o de negros terminó de formarlos. Letras jocosas y satíricas: «el chiste ingenuo y feliz enfrente de la tragedia jonda del quejío» (Emilio Jiménez Díaz). Aurelio y Pericón de Cádiz, Manuel Vargas y la Perla los grabaron en la primera mitad del siglo XX, y hasta Mairena dejó dos. Chano Lobato, su mayor cultor, los elevó a cante noble y recrea la venta de los cuadros que popularizó Pericón.

scenes.name: Las tonás: martinetes, carceleras y deblas
scenes.desc: Cantes sin acompañamiento, prueba de su antigüedad, en cuartetas octosílabas de intensa carga dramática y origen gitano indiscutible: son crónicas de la miseria, la cárcel y la persecución. Demófilo ya las daba en 1881 por «cantes viejos casi caídos en desuso»; en el siglo XIX hubo entre veintisiete y treinta y cuatro, cada una con el nombre de su creador. La más antigua es la de Tío Luis el de la Juliana, aguador y primer cantaor del que hay noticia (segunda mitad del siglo XVIII), conservada por Antonio Chacón y recreada por Pepe de la Matrona; se le atribuye también la toná de los pajaritos, que recuerda la tonada sefardí de los bilbilicos. Los martinetes toman el nombre del martillo de la fragua, aunque es difícil cantar mientras se forja: Tío Juane de Jerez montaba una fragua en escena en los setenta y ochenta, y Antonio el Bailarín creó su baile con martillo y yunque; la familia fragüera más antigua es la de los Cantorales de Cádiz, que Silverio visitaba. Las carceleras cantan la prisión y servían para pasar mensajes en romaní desde las rejas. La debla, único palo con nombre romaní («diosa»), es religiosa, casi perdida y muy difícil; llegó a hoy por Tomás Pavón en los cuarenta y la recuperó Antonio Mairena.

scenes.name: Las sevillanas
scenes.desc: Nacen de las seguidillas castellanas, que en Sevilla se hicieron más vivas y fáciles de repetir: cuatro coplas para bailar en pareja un galanteo, con temas andaluces, amorosos o rocieros (corraleras, rocieras, bíblicas, de feria, marineras, romeras). Lorca recogió una del siglo XVIII. Su gran auge comercial llegó en los setenta, con millones de discos que daban envidia a los flamencos; las han grabado con jondura Manuel Vallejo, la Niña de los Peines, la Paquera de Jerez, el Turronero, Chiquetete y Camarón.

scenes.name: El fandango
scenes.desc: Muy apreciado por su musicalidad y fácil de interpretar, no es un palo básico pero no es menor: la vieja división entre cantes grandes y chicos está obsoleta, y la jondura la pone el intérprete, no la antigüedad del palo. Canto para bailar de origen muy antiguo e incierto (Corominas lo deriva del portugués fado; hay quien le ve un lejano origen árabe), aparece por escrito en un entremés de 1705 y lo describe el deán Manuel Martí en 1712; en el siglo XIX fue el cante y baile nacional español, y a finales de siglo se aflamencó en Andalucía y dejó de bailarse. De él salen las granaínas, las malagueñas y los cantes de Levante, y hay fandangos propios en Lucena, Cabra, Puente Genil, Jaén, Granada o Almería. Su apogeo en la ópera flamenca lo desprestigió tanto que a cantaores como Pepe Menese les parece un insulto que se lo pidan; desde los años ochenta se revaloriza.

facts.title: "Man Dress" Controversy (November 1970 - June 1971)
facts.body: David Bowie's decision to wear a full-length blue dress on the original cover of *The Man Who Sold the World* album in November 1970 was a highly controversial move in America. At the time, Bowie had little reputation in the US, and the country was not "ready for a feminized rocker." This led to record stores refusing to stock the album until RCA Records provided an alternative cover, and even an incident where a gun was pulled on Bowie in Texas. "America, not ready for a guy wearing a dress."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 1
facts.name: David Bowie

facts.title: Manager Tony DeFries' Early Guidance (1970-1972)
facts.body: Tony DeFries, a solicitor by profession, signed on as Bowie's manager in 1970 when Bowie was a struggling young singer. Within approximately 18 months, DeFries secured Bowie a new deal with RCA records and proceeded to transform him into an international star. The entirety of Bowie's early 1970s career, including the iconic Ziggy Stardust era, was carefully guided by DeFries.
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Mighty Managers of Rock
facts.name: David Bowie

facts.title: Interview in Jeremy Magazine (1970)
facts.body: In January 1970, David Bowie became one of the first pop stars to be interviewed by Jeremy, a gay magazine. Although the article itself did not focus on his sexuality, the mere fact of his appearance in a gay publication was considered radical, especially given that just three years prior, being gay was still a jailable offense in the UK. "the very fact that he appeared in a game egg was pretty radical."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Early Days of LGBTQ Rock
facts.name: David Bowie

facts.title: Hype Costumes (1970)
facts.body: In 1970, with his band Hype, Bowie began experimenting with stage costumes. They wore superhero outfits made from shiny material, thigh-high boots, and Bowie's own costume included a cape and the word "rainbow man" sewn on his chest, a stark contrast to the hippie fashion of the time. "In 1970, around the time Mark Bowen was gaining fame with Ride-A-White Swan, Bowie had a band called Hype. They began appearing in interesting costumes."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock
facts.name: David Bowie

facts.title: Golden Period - 1970-1983
facts.body: Bowie experienced an incredibly prolific and impactful "golden period" from 1970 to 1983, during which he released 13 albums, many of which became not only classics but milestones in rock history. "He had a golden period that stretched roughly from 1970 through to 1983, 13 albums in those 13 years, and many of them remained not just classics, but milestones in the history of rock."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Why Bowie Still Matters - Part 2

facts.title: The Beatles Sell Their Share to ATV Music (By January 1970)
facts.body: Following a dispute with ATV over their publishing share, and after their manager Allen Klein failed to secure the desired deal, The Beatles sold their remaining stake in Northern Songs to ATV Music. By January 1970, ATV owned 99% of The Beatles' publishing. This financial tension significantly contributed to the band's breakup a few months later. "Very, very long story short, they did not get the deal they wanted, so the Beatles sold their piece of Northern Songs to ATV. By January 1970, ATV owned 99% of the Beatles' publishing. This financial tension went a long ways towards the Beatles breaking up a few months later."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Buying Catalogues - A Primer
facts.name: The Beatles

facts.title: Dave Grohl's Father Covered the Kent State Massacre (May 1970)
facts.body: In 1970, the Grohl family lived in Niles, Ohio (near Columbus). Dave's father James Grohl was a reporter for the Scripps News Agency and was assigned to cover anti-Vietnam War protests at Kent State University on May 1, 1970 — and was present when the National Guard opened fire, killing four students. James Grohl won several awards for his on-the-spot reporting, earning a major promotion and reassignment to Washington D.C., where Dave grew up and discovered music. "Had it not been for the National Guard killing four unarmed students at Kent State, who knows if we'd ever have heard of Dave Grohl?"
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: 10 Unusual Things About Nirvana
facts.name: Nirvana

facts.title: Early Uses in Music Criticism (1970-1971)
facts.body: The term "punk" began appearing in music criticism in the early 1970s; Lester Bangs called Iggy Pop a "stooge punk" in Cream Magazine (December 1970), and Dave Marsh referred to Question Mark and the Mysterians as "purveyors of punk rock" in Cream (May 1971). Alan Vega's band Suicide also adopted the term for their "punk masses" gigs. "In December 1970, the Detroit-based music magazine called Cream ran an article from a critic named Lester Banks who referred to Iggy Pop as that stooge punk."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 3
facts.name: Punk Rock

facts.title: Catalog Ownership Pre-1970
facts.body: Material released by The Rolling Stones before 1970 was owned by Abko Records, run by Allan Klein. This complicated the sampling clearance for The Verve's "Bittersweet Symphony," as Decca Records, which held the copyright to The Rolling Stones Songbook, did not control all the necessary rights. "Material release before 1970 was owned by Abco Records, run by Alan Klein, who had succeeded Andrew Geoldem as the Stones manager."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Dominant Force in 1970
facts.body: In 1970, rock and roll was considered "king" of the music landscape. It cultivated a serious critical discourse, with journalists writing in-depth articles about the genre, contrasting sharply with the perception of Top 40 music as "sugary, sweet pop" or "country-ish soft rock" listened to by older generations. "Rock and Roll was king and Top 40 evoked images of sugary, sweet pop or maybe some country-ish soft rock. Rock was king and it had bred a slew of journalists and critics that wrote very serious articles about a genre of music that they believed we should all take very seriously."

facts.body: The classic lineup of The Velvet Underground was shattered when Lou Reed left the group after a performance consisting of two sets at Max's Kansas City in New York on August 23, 1970, marking an abrupt end to their initial phase. facts.title: Internal Dysfunctions and Financial Hardship (1970)

"Motucker was expecting a child and she was absent from a lot of gigs. Sterling Morrison had grown bored and withdrawn and was barely speaking to anyone."

facts.title: Early Print Musical Reference (1970)
facts.body: The earliest verified print reference to "heavy metal" in a musical context appeared on February 7, 1970, in Cream Magazine. Music critic Lester Bangs described The Guess Who as "heavy metal robots," though this was intended as an insult rather than a definitive genre label. "They're quite refreshing in the wake of all the heavy metal robots of the year past."

facts.title: Birth through Devil's Triad (1970)
facts.body: Heavy metal is often considered by some to have originated in 1970 with Black Sabbath's debut album and title track. This birth was characterized by Tony Iomi's distinctive use of the tri tone—a flattened fifth played with a trill and distortion—an adaptation inspired by Gustav Holst's "Mars, the Bringer of War." "For some, this is the birth of heavy metal."

facts.title: American Debut at The Troubadour (September 12, 1970)
facts.body: Elton John made his pivotal American debut at The Troubadour on September 12, 1970, introduced by Neil Diamond. The club was packed with record executives eager to find the next big star. Reflecting on Doug Weston's death in 1999, Elton John stated that his "whole life came alive that night, musically, emotionally, everything," transforming him from a fan to an accepted musician and turning him into a star within a week in Los Angeles. "My whole life came alive that night, musically, emotionally, everything. It was like everything I had been waiting for suddenly happened."
facts.episode: Ep. 41 - The Impact of The Troubadour on 1970s Popular Culture
facts.name: Elton John

facts.title: Role in "Two Morrow" (1970)
facts.body: As a member of the pop group Two Morrow, Olivia Newton-John recorded an album and starred in a sci-fi musical fantasy film also titled "Two Morrow." This was her last major film role for eight years, until "Grease." "The Co-Ed group would record an album and star in a Barbara like sci-fi musical fantasy film called Two Morrow."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: Country Roads and Summer Nights Edition Part 1
facts.name: Olivia Newton-John

facts.title: Chrissie Hynde's Kent State Experience (May 4, 1970)
facts.body: Chrissie Hynde was a student at Kent State University on May 4, 1970, when the shootings occurred. She witnessed the events, knew one of the students who was killed, and vividly recalled hearing the shots and being carried off campus. Her memories also include the burning down of the ROTC building by students in protest of the Cambodia invasion, and the presence of both ROTC members (teenagers given loaded rifles) and the Ohio National Guard. "Well, yes. They killed four people and they closed down the university and the National Guard were surrounding a building which we, the student body, had burnt down a few days earlier in a protest when Nixon invaded Cambodia."
facts.episode: Ep. 43 - Music and The Kent State Massacre of May 4, 1970
facts.name: The Pretenders

facts.title: Inspiration from Kent State (1970)
facts.body: The killings at Kent State profoundly affected Chrissie Hynde, leading her to drop out of school and abandon her plans for an art degree. Although she initially drifted, the experience eventually set her on a path that led to her career as a rock star. "It would be inaccurate to say that the killings at Kent State led Chrissy Hine to rock and roll. Many may have put her on the path because she dropped out of school and abandoned her plans to get a degree in art after the shootings."
facts.episode: Ep. 43 - Music and The Kent State Massacre of May 4, 1970
facts.name: The Pretenders

facts.title: Accidental Death of Chauffeur (January 4, 1970)
facts.body: On January 4, 1970, outside the Red Lion Pub near London, Keith Moon's car was pelted with rocks and bottles by a crowd of skinheads. His chauffeur, Neil Bowen, stepped out to try and calm the situation. In a panic, Moon, who did not have a driver's license, jumped behind the wheel and hit the accelerator, trapping and dragging Bowen beneath the car, leading to his death in hospital. "On January 4, 1970, Keith ran into an angry crowd outside the Red Lion Pub near London, a group of skinheads went after Moon and his Bentley pelting it with rocks and bottles."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Ahmet Ertegun's Urgency for "Ohio" (1970)
facts.body: The president of CSNY's record company, named Almitard in the transcript (likely Ahmet Ertegun), demonstrated extraordinary urgency by flying the master tape of "Ohio" on a red-eye flight from Los Angeles to New York. His demand for immediate release led to the strategic decision to pull "Teach Your Children" from the charts, despite its potential to reach number one, to ensure "Ohio" was released without delay. "President of our record company, a wonderful man named Almitard, who was him Los Angeles that night when we finished recording and he took tape and flew to New York on the red eye. He said, I want this out now."

facts.title: Festival Express Performance - Toronto (June 27, 1970)
facts.body: Janis Joplin delivered an electrifying performance in Toronto, described by Rolling Stone writers David Dalton and Jonathan Cott as a "Bacchanalian little red riding hood with her bag full of tequila and lemons lurching from car to car like some tropical bird with streaming feathers." Canadian writer Bill Damper noted that her one-hour set changed the value of the $16 admission, generating enough personality and electricity to light up the stadium. "It was worth that much and more to see in here Janice Joplin, Long Haired, Swivel Hipped, Janice Joplin singing with the insistence and power of a pile driver and generating enough personality and electricity to light up a stadium all by herself."

facts.title: Louisville Concert Reception (June 12, 1970)

"Janice looked out on the crowd and she didn't see what she might call her people in the front row and she said, shit, man, why do those country club chicks and their panty girdles always have to be sitting in the front rows?"

"It was worth that much and more to see in here Janice Joplin, Long Haired, Swivel Hipped, Janice Joplin singing with the insistence and power of a pile driver and generating enough personality and electricity to light up a stadium all by herself."

facts.title: Louisville Concert Reception (June 12, 1970)
facts.body: During a show at Freedom Hall in Louisville, Kentucky, a conservative southern town, Janis initially saw "country club chicks" in the front rows and expressed her frustration. Despite a slow start, her performance led the crowd to go "bonkers," with dancing and pushing toward the stage, causing friction with security guards. "Janice looked out on the crowd and she didn't see what she might call her people in the front row and she said, shit, man, why do those country club chicks and their panty girdles always have to be sitting in the front rows?"

facts.title: The Rural Purge (1970-1971)
facts.body: Under the leadership of Fred Silverman, who took over CBS in 1970-1971, the network underwent a significant programming shift known as the "rural purge." This initiative systematically canceled any show perceived as "remotely country," regardless of its ratings, including popular programs like The Johnny Cash Show, Petticoat Junction, The Beverly Hillbillies, The Red Skelton Show, Green Acres, and even The Ed Sullivan Show. The move was replaced by "urban friendly programming" such as All in the Family, MASH, and The Mary Tyler Moore Show, driven by a desire to target more heavily populated areas for higher ratings. "he gutted the network of any show that seemed remotely country. It did not matter what the ratings were."

facts.name: CBS Records (Canada)

facts.title: Decline by 1970 - Physical and Professional Deterioration
facts.body: By 1970, Jim Morrison's personal situation and The Doors' status had become very complicated. His severe alcoholism and drug use made him an impossible person to work with, causing a drastic physical deterioration; he grew a beard, dressed disheveled, and took on the appearance of a "ragged hippie." To conceal his condition from the public, photographs used for singles, album covers, and interviews from this period often utilized older archival images from 1968 and 1969. "Jim Morrison, como persona, había de generado muchísimo, sus problemas con el alcolismo y con las drogas, la hacía una persona completamente imposible para trabajar."

facts.title: Later Career and Diverse Activities (Post-1970)
facts.body: For several decades after 1970, Johnny Otis continued to tour with his old collaborators, including Marie Adams who rejoined in 1972. Beyond music, he hosted his own radio show dedicated to black musical history and interviewed old musicians, wrote more books (including a cookbook and art collection), ran an organic apple juice company and food store, painted blues artists in a style inspired by African art and Picasso, and served as pastor of a broad-minded Pentecostal church that affirmed LGBT individuals and included Buddhist and Jewish congregants. "For the next few decades, Otis combined touring with as many of his old collaborators as possible. Marie Adams, for example, rejoined the band in 1972, with having his own radio show in which he told people about black musical history and interviewed as many old musicians as he could."

facts.title: Eccentric Persona and Androgynous Style (1970)

He also shifted from intellectual folk lyrics to more loving, sexually explicit, romantic, and melancholic themes, which became hallmarks of glam music. facts.title: Second Album
facts.body: Named after their living quarters in Detroit, this album was recorded in Los Angeles. The recording process was characterized by extensive drug use, including the band's first experience with cocaine. The album was recorded largely live off the floor with minimal overdubs to capture their raw live sound, with its seven songs recorded in sequence like a live gig. Released in July 1970, *Fun House* is retrospectively considered the best representation of The Stooges' sound, though at the time it was savaged by critics and commercially unsuccessful. "That whole record was recorded live off the floor."

facts.title: Prioritizing "Ohio" Release (1970)
facts.body: The president of CSNY's record company, Ahmet Ertegun (transcribed as Almitard), flew the master tape of "Ohio" on a red-eye flight from Los Angeles to New York to ensure its immediate release. This decision led to pulling "Teach Your Children," a song already climbing the charts and poised to be a number one hit, to get "Ohio" out quickly. "President of our record company, a wonderful man named Almitard, who was him Los Angeles that night when we finished recording and he took tape and flew to New York on the red eye. He said, I want this out now."

facts.title: "Ohio" Single Cover Art (1970)
facts.body: The single for "Ohio" featured a striking cover photograph of the United States Constitution riddled with four bullet holes, a direct and powerful visual commentary on the Kent State shootings. "Cover was a picture of the Constitution with four bullet holes in it."

facts.title: Kent State Impact on CSNY's Future (1970)
facts.body: The internal conflicts within CSNY were legendary, and the tour for their "Deja Vu" album was cut short due to these issues and technical problems at their first show in Denver on May 12, 1970, where Neil Young reportedly threw down his guitar and threatened to leave. David Crosby and Neil Young were at their road manager's house in Northern California, reassessing the band's future, when Young was inspired to write "Ohio" after seeing the Life Magazine photo. "The tour to support that record was over before it ever started. The internal conflict in CSNY is rather legendary."

facts.title: Misinterpretation of "Ohio" in Akron (1970)
facts.body: Johnny Andrews of WHLO in Akron, Ohio, played "Ohio" extensively, where it reached number one by mid-July. However, his interpretation was that the song was a message to protesters to "cool it for a while or get shot," which he believed was "the proper thing," completely misconstruing its anti-war and anti-violence message. "Our interpretation was that it was a rock group giving a message to protesters to cool it for a while or get shot."
facts.episode: Ep. 43 - Music and The Kent State Massacre of May 4, 1970
facts.name: Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young

facts.title: Stephen Stills' Initial Hesitation with "Ohio" (1970)
facts.body: After "Ohio" was recorded, Stephen Stills expressed some reservations about the lyrics. He found it hard to believe that the National Guard would open fire with live ammunition, thinking some members might have been told they were carrying blanks. "Even Stephen Stills was not so sure about the lyrics. He thought surely there were some members of the guard who were told that they did not have live ammunition."

facts.title: Triple Album
facts.body: This was George Harrison's debut triple album as a solo artist, released "out of the gate" after The Beatles' breakup. It was co-produced by Phil Spector and featured a strong backing lineup including Eric Clapton, Billy Preston, Gary Wright, Ringo Starr, and all four members of Badfinger. facts.title: Original Intent
facts.body: According to lead singer Burton Cummings, "American Woman" was not originally intended to be anti-American or anti-war, despite being widely interpreted as such during the Vietnam War era. "According to Burton Cummings, the lead singer for the guest who at that time American woman was not intended to be anti-American or anti-war although many people interpreted both of these ways."
facts.episode: Ep. 45 - Oh, Canada! Canada's Rock Music Industry in the 70s
facts.name: American Woman

facts.title: Original Meaning
facts.body: Burton Cummings stated that the song "American Woman" was actually about a Canadian man feeling intimidated by what he perceived as more assertive American women. "Cummings said it was really about a Canadian guy being intimidated by slightly more assertive American women."
facts.episode: Ep. 45 - Oh, Canada! Canada's Rock Music Industry in the 70s
facts.name: American Woman

facts.title: Political Interpretation
facts.body: Despite Burton Cummings' stated intent, during the Vietnam War era, "American Woman" was widely interpreted by many listeners as a political statement due to lyrics referencing "war machine" and "ghetto scene." "given that this is the Vietnam War era, regardless of what Cummings said it was supposed to be, many people did interpret American woman as political."
facts.episode: Ep. 45 - Oh, Canada! Canada's Rock Music Industry in the 70s
facts.name: American Woman

facts.title: Signature Guitar Riff
facts.body: The song "American Woman" features an instantly recognizable opening guitar riff that plays a crucial role in its distinct identity and overall impact. "Lyric's aside, the opening guitar riff makes the song instantly recognizable."
facts.episode: Ep. 45 - Oh, Canada! Canada's Rock Music Industry in the 70s
facts.name: American Woman

facts.title: Riff Origin
facts.body: The iconic guitar riff for "American Woman" was created spontaneously on the spot by Randy Bachman, who played it to signal Burton Cummings, who was outside the curling rink trying to buy records, to get back on stage. "Cummings said that that riff was just made up on the spot by Randy Beckman."
facts.episode: Ep. 45 - Oh, Canada! Canada's Rock Music Industry in the 70s
facts.name: American Woman

facts.title: Lyric Creation
facts.body: Upon hearing Randy Bachman's impromptu riff, Burton Cummings ran to the stage and, in what he described as a "Bob Dylan-esque stream of consciousness moment," began spontaneously spouting out lyrics, initially aiming just for rhymes. "Cummings hears that riff, runs up to the stage and what he describes as a Bob Dylan S. stream of consciousness moment. He just starts spouting out some lyrics."
facts.episode: Ep. 45 - Oh, Canada! Canada's Rock Music Industry in the 70s
facts.name: American Woman

facts.title: Bootleg Recording Preservation
facts.body: Fortuitously, a kid in the audience was recording the show with a tape recorder to create a bootleg. The band convinced him to give them the tape containing their "American Woman" jam, thereby preserving a crucial moment in rock history that became a number one hit. "As luck would have it, there was a kid in the audience who had a tape recorder because he was going to make a bootleg tape of the show. And the band convinced him to give them the tape with their American woman jam on it."
facts.episode: Ep. 45 - Oh, Canada! Canada's Rock Music Industry in the 70s
facts.name: American Woman

facts.title: Billboard #1 Hit
facts.body: "American Woman" achieved the number one position on the Billboard Hot 100 chart on May 9, 1970, marking a significant commercial success for the band. "This song American woman went to number one on the Billboard Hot 100 on May 9, 1970."
facts.episode: Ep. 45 - Oh, Canada! Canada's Rock Music Industry in the 70s
facts.name: American Woman

facts.title: Reaction to #1 Hit
facts.body: Burton Cummings recounted that the band received the news of "American Woman" hitting number one on the charts while staying at a Holiday Inn in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, leading to such excitement that they jumped on the beds until they broke it. "Bert Cumming said that when they found out they were at a holiday in in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. Back then you found out on Wednesdays where your record was on the charts and Randy Beckman took the call, told the band and then they jumped up and down on the bed so hard that they broke it."

facts.name: American Woman

facts.body: This album was a genuine revolution in the music industry and an authentic masterpiece. It was recorded in one day and mixed in another, with a budget of 600 pounds. Technically, the recording is a disaster, showing noise, saturated sounds, and cuts, which is understandable given the limited time and budget. Despite these technical flaws, the public was intelligent enough to appreciate its distinct, fresh, new, and spontaneous sound, turning it into a revolution. This album's raw spontaneity and technical disregard greatly influenced the punk movement. It is officially considered the starting point of heavy metal, not just musically, but aesthetically. "musicalmente son relativamente cuestionables porque su primer disco se grabó en un día con otro día de remetlas con un prosopuesto de 600 libras."

facts.body: This album, released in 1970, features the song "Black Sabbath," which prominently showcases Tony Iomi's distinctive use of the tri tone. Played with a trill and added distortion, this recording is considered by some to be a foundational moment in the birth of heavy metal music. "In 1970, Black Sabbath released an album called Black Sabbath, that included a song called Black Sabbath. And you can clearly hear Iomi's tri tone played with a little bit of a trill."

facts.title: Kent State Student on May 4, 1970
facts.body: Joe Walsh, despite having already released two records with the James Gang and being on the verge of touring with The Who, was enrolled in classes at Kent State on May 4, 1970, and was present during the shootings. He first enrolled in 1965, attending full-time for less than a year, then part-time for about six years. "I think we were still making the blueprint for what it meant to be a rock star. It's kind of like the major league baseball players who had to take jobs to sell appliances or life insurance or something like that in the off season."
facts.episode: Ep. 43 - Music and The Kent State Massacre of May 4, 1970
facts.name: Joe Walsh

facts.title: Kent State Shootings' Profound Impact (1970)
facts.body: Joe Walsh, who majored in English and minored in music, stated that being at the shootings "affected me profoundly." This experience led him to view college differently and ultimately influenced his decision to pursue music as a full-time profession as the James Gang gained momentum, concluding, "I decided that maybe I don't need a degree that bad." "Unfortunately, I was at the shootings. After that, I didn't look at college the same. Then the James Gang started to gather momentum and I decided I'd try pursuing music as a profession."

facts.name: Joe Walsh

facts.title: Dick Cavett Show Appearance (1970)
facts.body: On May 25, 1970, Ali appeared on The Dick Cavett Show, where he famously articulated his reasons for draft resistance. When asked about going to jail, he connected his personal sacrifice to the broader struggle of black people, stating, "So why should I worry about going to a little old jail to free my poor people who've been catching hell here for 400 years?" This statement received significant applause from the studio audience. "So why should I worry about going to a little old jail to free my poor people who've been catching hell here for 400 years?"

facts.body: In September 1970, a federal judge restored Ali's right to fight, ending his three-year boxing ban. Despite California Governor Ronald Reagan's refusal to allow a "draft Dodger" to box in his state and similar opposition from Georgia's governor, a fight was approved in Atlanta by its mayor. facts.title: Formation and Style (1970-1975)
facts.body: The Razberries, a group from Cleveland, were active from 1970 to 1975. They produced songs with melodies reminiscent of the bubblegum pop side of British glam rock, but distinctively incorporated elements of the classic American garage band sound, which also foreshadowed the new wave music that emerged later in the decade. "They existed for five years, 1970 to 1975. And during that period, they released some killer songs with melodies that sort of ran parallel with the bubblegumny pop side of British glam rock."

Franklin's version, a full-on gospel hymn, reached number 6 on the Hot 100 and number 1 on the R&B chart. "A year after Simon and Garfunkel took bridge over troubled water to number 1."

facts.body: This song was Simon & Garfunkel's biggest hit before they broke up, bidding farewell to the 1960s. It is essentially a gospel song and was replaced at number one in 1970 by The Beatles' "Let It Be." Aretha Franklin covered it, and it defeated The Carpenters' "Close to You" and The Guess Who's "American Woman" for the year-end title. "Bridge over troubled water is essentially a gospel song."
